description: Liwaza Discovery is the team for Liwaza students in grades 6 and 7. On 14–15 November 2026 we will tell a clear story for other school-age space fans about NASA hardware left on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space: what it was built to do, the science it made possible, and what remains of it today. The project will be a short illustrated story or video. Join this team only if you are in the Liwaza Discovery group.
summary:
Our presentation is about space exploration, the Moon and Mars.

The Moon is Earth's closest neighbour. It is about 384,400 km away from Earth. Its surface is grey and covered with craters, mountains and dust. It has no air and no water, and it is the only place.

The Moon is very important for us. It gives light at night, it causes the tides in the oceans, and it helps scientists to understand how our solar system was formed.

In 1969, the Apollo 11 mission sent three astronauts to the Moon: Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins and Buzz Aldrin. Neil Armstrong was the first man to walk on the Moon. He said the famous sentence: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

The astronauts left a laser mirror on the Moon. Scientists on Earth still send laser beams to this mirror today. This helps them to measure the exact distance between the Earth and the Moon, and to discover that the Moon is slowly moving away from us.

Mars is the red planet. It is called red because of the iron in its rocks and dust. Mars is farther from the Sun than Earth, and it is very cold and dry. It has the largest volcano in the solar system, called Olympus Mons.

Scientists want to know if there was life on Mars in the past. For this reason, they sent a robot called Opportunity to Mars in 2004. Opportunity was supposed to work for only 90 days, but it worked for almost 15 years. It explored the planet, took thousands of photos, studied rocks and searched for signs of water.
